text:
Droit de la famille — 18522

2018 QCCS
1031

JG 2551

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-12-329265-155

DATE:

March 15, 2018

______________________________________________________________________

PRESIDING:  THE HONOURABLE LUKASZ GRANOSIK, J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

M. A.

Plaintiff

v.

S. R.

Defendant

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

(divorce)

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

The parties were
married on December 31, 2007 in Israel and separated on November 13, 2015 in
Montreal. Madame was born in Israel and came to Canada thanks to the
sponsorship by Monsieur, a Canadian and Israeli citizen. Four children were
born in City A of this marriage: X, Y, Z and A, respectively
in 2008, 2010, 2011 and 2014. Unfortunately, X and Z are autistic.

[
2
]

The union was a
traditional one, and although Madame used to work in Israel as a teacher and holds
a B.A. degree in music, she only took care of the household and the children
during the marriage. Monsieur owned a company, of which he was the sole shareholder
and administrator, distributing various health and miscellaneous products to
drugstores and convenience stores. His revenues allowed the family to have quite
a comfortable standard of life
[1]
. They resided in City A but would
often visit Israel where their respective parents lived, as well as some of both
parties’ siblings. In 2014, they bought a house for almost $500,000 and
proceeded with extensive renovations. The older children recently started to
attend private or rabbinical schools, with additional resources involved to
support the specific needs of X and Z.

[
3
]

The separation
was quite turbulent. The police and security guards were involved and Monsieur even
spent a few days in prison. Initially, a shared custody agreement was ratified
by this court but since February 9, 2016, Madame has had sole custody of the
children, with Monsieur having limited access rights. Monsieur was also ordered
to pay child support, initially, in the amount of approximately $1,000 monthly
and had to pay 60% of special expenses.

[
4
]

The access
arrangements and the exact amount of child support have varied throughout the
evolution of the file, but not in a significant manner. Unfortunately, Monsieur
stopped paying child support, stopped paying mortgage and home
expenses, and the children’s special expenses in June 2016 altogether, with the
exception of one payment of child support. In 2017, the mortgage lender, a
bank, repossessed the family house.

[
5
]

In July 2016, a
signalement

was filed to the Director of Youth Protection (DYP). After verification and
analysis, the DYP considered the facts founded and asked the Court of Quebec to
declare the security and development of all four children to be in danger (
compromission
),
in accordance with
Section 38
c) of the
Youth Protection Act
[2]
:

38.
For the purposes
of this Act, the security or development of a child is considered to be in
danger if the child is abandoned, neglected, subjected to psychological
ill-treatment or sexual or physical abuse, or if the child has serious
behavioural disturbances.

In this Act,

(…)

(
c
)

“
psychological ill-treatment
” refers to
a situation in which a child is seriously or repeatedly subjected to behaviour
on the part of the child’s parents or another person that could cause harm to
the child, and the child’s parents fail to take the necessary steps to put an
end to the situation. Such behaviour includes in particular indifference,
denigration, emotional rejection, excessive control, isolation, threats,
exploitation, particularly if the child is forced to do work disproportionate
to the child’s capacity, and exposure to conjugal or domestic violence;

[
6
]

Both
parties agreed with the recommended measures and a decision was rendered accordingly
on March 27, 2017, by which the Court of Quebec, Youth Division, among other
conclusions and as an interim order, granted the custody of all the children to
Madame and determined that access rights to Monsieur were to be decided specifically
by the DYP. The trial on the merits was scheduled for January 8, 2018, but as the
divorce case was to be heard in February, 2018, the Court of Quebec postponed its
hearing until April 3, 2018, with a pre-trial conference to take place on March
13, 2018.

[
7
]

On
October 19, 2016, the Superior Court increased the child support to $1,900 per
month, which Monsieur never paid. On April 20, 2017, by another interim order, the
Court agreed with Madame to suspend X’s access to Monsieur and at the same time
dismissed Monsieur’s safeguard motion to extend access and the use of the
family van. Since then, DYP is monitoring the
access rights which have been increased lately, although they are different
with regards to each child of the parties. It is worth noting
that despite the context, Madame never asked for, and Monsieur was never
ordered, to pay spousal support.

QUESTIONS

[
8
]

This
case raises the following questions:

-

What is the extent of this Court’s jurisdiction, where the Court of
Quebec applying the
Youth Protection Act
has already declared the
well-being of children compromised and is still in charge of the file?

-

What are the financial consequences of the divorce, including the child
support and the cancelation of the arears as well as Monsieur’s revenue?

-

Can Madame be allowed to emigrate to Israel with the four children, without
Monsieur’s consent?

ANALYSIS

Jurisdiction

[
9
]

Although custody
per se
has not been an issue raised in this trial, the
access rights by Monsieur, which is one of its features, certainly were. To
that effect, Article 37 of the
Code of civil procedure
(CCP) provides :

37.
The Court of
Quebec has jurisdiction, to the exclusion of the Superior Court, to hear and
determine applications in adoption matters.

In other youth matters, jurisdiction and procedure are determined by
special Acts.

If an adoption or youth protection matter is already before the Court
of Quebec, it may rule on any related application concerning child custody,
emancipation, the exercise of parental authority, suppletive tutorship or
tutorship requested by the director of youth protection.

[
10
]

Here, the Court of Quebec, Youth Division, is implicitly
deferring the decision on access rights to the Superior Court and postponed its
hearing to a later date to allow this Court to hear the divorce case. The reference
in both
procès-verbaux
of the Youth Court to reconvening only after
February 9, 2018, is quite clear.
[3]

The testimony of the DYP representative, the social worker Karen Chawkin, was
to the same effect. The Court of Quebec is well aware of Mother’s request to
move to Israel. Both parties ask this Court to rule on that subject.

[
11
]

The authorities on that specific question are not very
abundant. In
Protection de la jeunesse — 172344
,

Justice Daigle wrote that the jurisdiction of the Court
of Quebec must follow the declaration of
compromission
:

[42] Tel que prévu à l’
article 91
de la
Loi sur la protection de la
jeunesse
,
la Cour du Québec peut se prononcer sur les mesures applicables à
l’égard de l’enfant dont la situation lui est soumise. Elle doit cependant au
préalable conclure que la sécurité ou le développement de l’enfant est
compromis.

[43] Dans un tel cas, la compétence de la Cour du Québec de statuer
accessoirement sur la garde d’un enfant prime sur la compétence générale de la
Cour supérieure dans le contexte d’une demande de protection ou d’adoption. En
fait,
dans ce contexte, le débat en moins un de juridiction, […] que
d’opportunité. […] il demeure que le forum le plus approprié, dans les
circonstances, pour décider de la demande […] concernant la garde de l’enfant,
est la Cour du Québec.

[44] Mais qu’en est-il lorsque le Tribunal en arrive à la conclusion
que la sécurité et le développement de l’enfant ne sont pas ou plus compromis?

[45] Le Tribunal est d’avis que la compétence de la Cour du Québec
quant à la question de garde d’enfant, est un accessoire au pouvoir exclusif
qu’elle détient en vertu de la
Loi sur la protection de la jeunesse
.
[4]

(Reference omitted)

[
12
]

In 2015, Mes

Perron et

Labrecque Tremblay
wrote a comprehensive and interesting summary of this question, but
left it unanswered :

À la lumière de ce nouvel article, nous
croyons que celui-ci aura certains impacts bénéfiques dans l'optique d'une
meilleure administration de la justice.

Toutefois, il appert que certaines
questions demeurent et devront être clarifiées afin d'avoir un aperçu complet
de l'application des nouveaux pouvoirs qui sont conférés aux juges de la Cour
du Québec, Chambre de la jeunesse.
[5]

[
13
]

In three judgments -
quite impressive by the depth of the analysis - Justice Dugré opines that the Court
of Quebec has the exclusive jurisdiction in such cases.
[6]

[
14
]

Finally,
in

Droit de
la famille — 163483
, the Court of Quebec speaks of co-existence of
jurisdictions between the two courts, rather than the exclusive jurisdiction of
the Court of Quebec :

[24]        La
compétence attribuée à la Cour du Québec en matière de garde est liée à la
saisine en adoption ou en vertu de la
Loi sur
la protection de la jeunesse
,
laquelle est indépendante du statut matrimonial des parents.  Il
s’agit d’une compétence qui s’exerce dans le cadre restreint de la juridiction
de la Cour du Québec dans les matières relatives à la jeunesse.

[25]        Cette
distinction est fondamentale et, jumelée aux effets bénéfiques incontestables,
justifie la coexistence quant aux compétences en matière de garde d'enfant
entre la Cour supérieure et la Cour du Québec, sans égard au statut matrimonial
des parents.

[7]

[
15
]

Here, it must be noted
that the parties recognize the jurisdiction of the Superior Court, and
underscore that the Court of Quebec has postponed its hearing awaiting this
Court’s decision on the very issue at stake and that the DYP leaves it for this
Court’s discretion to determine the matter in dispute. Nonetheless, if this is
a question of jurisdiction
ratione materiae
, the Court is not bound by parties’
admissions and must determine this issue.
Parties should not be able, by agreement, to contract
out of the appropriate jurisdiction.

[
16
]

In dealing with this matter,
the Court must first underline that Article 37 CCP, in its three distinct
paragraphs, deals with three different questions:

-  exclusive jurisdiction in adoption cases;

-  jurisdiction in other youth matters in accordance with the
applicable statutes;

- potential jurisdiction on different issues including
child custody, if matter is already before the Court of Quebec.

[
17
]

The Court emphasises
that this last third paragraph did not exist before the enactment of the
current CCP in 2016.
[8]

Without proceeding to a detailed analysis of the law, mainly because the
parties have declined the invitation to present substantive arguments with
regards to this particular question, the Court is of the opinion
[9]
that

there is an overlapping or a concurrent jurisdiction between the Court of
Quebec and the Superior Court, and that this overlap must serve the best
interests of the children. This is mainly because of the use of a specific and different
language in the third paragraph. The absence of the adjective “
exclusive
”
in this part of the Article 37 leads to the conclusion that Court of Quebec does
not possess an exclusive jurisdiction over that matter.

[
18
]

In
Celgen
, the Supreme Court of Canada had
said the following about the statutory interpretation :

[21] (…) The words, if clear, will dominate; if not,
they yield to an interpretation that best meets the overriding purpose of the
statute.
[10]

[
19
]

In the case at hand, the Court considers that
the
words
of Article 37 CPP are
clear
but even if they weren’t, it is
the expediency and the early referral that will determine which court decides the
custody and access rights. Here, this Court conducted a four-day trial, heard
parents and two social workers and other witnesses about the situation of the
children and is able to comment on it.

[
20
]

In application of this finding, the Court
underscores that Monsieur does not ask for custody but only wishes to extend
his access rights. Obviously, everyone agrees that it is beneficial to children
to maximize access to their father. Yet, the Court concludes that Monsieur’s
parental capacities are lacking (even though his sincerity and his love of the
children are not); not only does he discuss with the children the case at hand but
when they are ill,
[11]
instead of looking for treatment and help, he brings them back to Madame
earlier then he is supposed to in accordance with his access rights so she can
take care of the health issues. He refuses or neglects to proceed with the toilet training for A, to the point that 3½ year-old child is still
in diapers, which results in social and personal drawbacks for this little boy.
Moreover, the DYP proceedings concern mostly Monsieur’s
behavior and the Court of Quebec decision has uncontested probative value. Finally, Monsieur does not acknowledge any
wrongdoing or responsibility vis-à-vis the children, thus demonstrating lack of
maturity and introspection.

[
21
]

On the other hand, Madame is very much the
dominant and caring figure with all four children, attends correctly to all their
needs
[12]

and even the social worker qualifies her motivation and involvement as
“exceptional”
[13]

with regards to the special services provided to X and Z.

[
22
]

Therefore, the access rights shall remain as
they are, until the date of departure of Madame for Israel. This being said, the
DYP is invited to continue monitoring the situation closely in trying to
maximize the access by Monsieur as soon and as much possible to all the
children.

Child support, arrears and Monsieur’s revenue

[
23
]

Monsieur asks to cancel
the arrears of child support which have accumulated to $31,906.74 as it appears
from the latest Statement provided to the Court, and wants to calculate the
child support retroactively, based on his 2016 revenues of $26,000.
For the year 2017, Monsieur affirms that he did not have any income as
he did not work. In 2018 Monsieur started receiving social assistance.

[
24
]

Monsieur’s professional history is difficult
to
follow,
especially since the separation. He has been operating a company importing and
selling health products and various items to drugstores and
dépanneurs
,
with a single salesperson at his employment. First, in 2000, he had the company
A. In 2002, the name was [Company A]. In 2007, [Company B] was created and in
2008 the name changed to [Company C]. In 2009, the company became [Company D]
but since 2011, it was known as [Company E]. Finally, in 2013, [Company F] was
established.

[
25
]

Monsieur has always been
t
he administrator
and sole shareholder of these companies and their address remained the same throughout
the years. It could be inferred that since 2000 this company has existed under
different names in order to evade creditors, which is exactly Madame’s
contention. This is also supported by Monsieur’s accountant who candidly explained
that Monsieur has created [Company F] because he accumulated too much debt in
the previous company.

[
26
]

Madame estimated the cost of the family’s
lifestyle,
after
having moved in the newly purchased family house, at $10,000 a month. She
provided in her testimony a long list of recurring monthly expenses. Monsieur only
contradicted the value of the lease of one of three cars he had; instead of $900
as estimated by Madame, it was only $500. All the other expenses were not denied.

[
27
]

Monsieur founded his position mainly on the income
tax statements of his company. The Court finds that information has a limited
probative value. The accountant who testified on behalf of Monsieur did not
personally audit anything but only relied on the figures provided by his client.
Monsieur’s business involved a lot of cash transactions and the Court cannot rely
exclusively on the financial statements that Monsieur has provided, which are
incidentally not verified, to determine his income.

[
28
]

Madame also states that Monsieur was an
intermediary in a cash loan business in which he would be “moving” cash money
from
N.
, a Hassidic Jew residing in [City A - borough A], to
G.
,
another member of the Jewish community in City A, and that he would get 1% from
each party for a successful transaction. Monsieur acknowledges that he would
handle large amounts of cash money in plastic bags, but explains that he was
‘juggling’” his own loans with regards to his business. Monsieur does not
contest that there was a cash machine in the house, that he was using a safe and
that he possessed a firearm. Finally, he cannot explain why there were
documents in the house confirming wire transfers of large sums to foreign
jurisdictions.

[
29
]

In the Interim Consent
of March 9, 2016, Monsieur admitted making as much as $66,000 per year.
As for the current situation, Monsieur did not explain nor did he provide
any medical certificate or justification why he would not be able to work full-time
as an employee, especially since his company was inactive and did not produce anymore
revenues. He did not file any job
applications
with potential employers and he did
not testify about any search for work in any capacity
[14]
.

[
30
]

The Court can determine
Monsieur’s revenue in accordance with Article 446 CCP:

446.

If the
particulars in a prescribed document are incomplete or contested, or in any
circumstances it considers it necessary, the court may supplement the
information. The court may determine a parent’s income by considering, among
other things, the value of the parent’s assets and the income they generate or
could generate, as it considers appropriate.

[
31
]

The Court of Appeal
explains the application of this particular section in
Droit de la famille -

162999:

[25]

L’article 446
C.p.c
.
accorde au tribunal le pouvoir d’imputer un revenu à un parent aux fins du
calcul de la pension alimentaire. Ce pouvoir est généralement utilisé dans deux
circonstances. La première vise les cas où les informations données sur le
revenu d’un parent sont incomplètes ou erronées. La deuxième concerne les
situations où, même si les informations sont exactes, le revenu du parent est
inférieur à ce qu’il devrait être en fonction de sa capacité de travail
. Cela vise les cas où un parent adopte une démarche
professionnelle insouciante ou imprégnée de mauvaise foi, susceptible de
conséquences fâcheuses sur son obligation alimentaire. La jurisprudence
répertorie diverses situations : l’abandon d’un emploi, la diminution
volontaire du revenu, le refus de maximiser ses gains, la prise volontaire de
la retraite

et la réorientation de la
carrière. Chaque situation est évaluée à son mérite pour vérifier si, au regard
de toutes les circonstances, la décision du parent est raisonnable.

(References omitted)

[
32
]

In examining this
question, the Court must underline that Monsieur’s credibility is at best, doubtful.
He answered certain questions, even the simplest and non-leading, in
cross-examination, by comments: «it is a blatant lie” or “shame on you!”
addressed either to Madame or her lawyer. He acknowledged in his testimony that
the family planned to emigrate to Israel while in a sworn declaration
previously filed in the docket, he denied that very fact.
[15]
As another example of lack
of trustworthiness and therefore, credibility, Monsieur pretended that he did
not contest the change of custody because he said it would cost him too much
and provided in his testimony three different figures, for the amount his
lawyer would demand for that service: first $2,500, then $3,000 and finally $2,000
plus taxes. Within a few minutes, while explaining why is there a death
certificate in the Israeli official state register, he declared not being an
Israeli citizen, later, having only an Israeli citizenship number while not
being a citizen of that country and at the end acknowledging that he was
actually an Israeli citizen.

[
33
]

His declaration why
there is a death certificate to his name defies any logical explanation and the
fact that he would provide to the Israeli authorities a false first name when
he visited, is also questionable. Also, he stated that he abandoned the
inventory of his company while in the last corporate financial statement its
value was estimated at $55,773 in 2015. Not only is this highly unlikely, but
Monsieur did not explain why he let go of his company’s assets or why he wouldn’t
proceed with a fire sale of same.
He did not answer, when asked in cross-examination why, if he is
submerged with debt, continuously receiving demand letters from various collection
agencies and living off social assistance, he does not go bankrupt but chooses
to carry all the debts. He did not explain either why he is still paying
insurance for a warehouse where his inventory used to be stored. In general,
Monsieur gives the impression that he is looking to provide a good answer to
the question rather than true answer.

[
34
]

On the contrary, Madame’s
answers were clear, simple and very likely, given the complicated context of this
case. She convinces the Court that Monsieur was not only receiving income from
his company but that he was also being well paid when he acted as an
intermediary in the operations of “moving” large amounts of cash money.

[
35
]

Finally, Monsieur took a line of credit of $120,000
which he has spent by himself in 2015 and 2016. No receipts or
invoices
whatsoever
support Monsieur’s contention that this money was used to help his business.
The evidence only shows that municipal taxes for the family residence in the
beginning of 2016 were paid out of this line of credit.

[
36
]

His allegations that he is currently working for
free (and he seems to be working because at least on one occasion he couldn’t
take care of the children because he declared being outside of City A for
work), doesn’t pay rent, doesn’t pay his accountant, are hardly believable and,
given his overall lack of credibility, cannot be accepted on the balance of
probabilities. His current employer, the owner of a deli shop, did not comply
with a subpoena and did not come to testify and his current landlord did not
explain (except for the argument based on both parties’ ethnic origin, which is
not convincing at all) why only a few months ago he sent a demand letter to
Monsieur threatening him of eviction and suddenly he decided to let Monsieur
stay in an apartment for free, foregoing a monthly rent of almost $1,000.

[
37
]

In light of the above,
this is a clear case for the simultaneous application of the two situations
triggering the use of Article 446 CCP; Monsieur certainly downplays his real income
and also refuses to maximize his capacity to earn money and to hold an
employment.
The sudden demise of his business which
coincides with the separation is not explained in any convincing fashion.

[
38
]

Madame’s evidence is
thus preferred and the Court accepts that this family would possess a monthly
budget of about $10,000 net. This is the income that Monsieur did have and
could still earn today. Therefore, Madame’s request that this Court impute Monsieur’s
annual income at $100,000 gross is justified and actually quite conservative because
it is on the lower end of the spectrum of financial possibilities. The child support
for 2018 will be therefore calculated based on this figure.

[
39
]

Given that conclusion
and lack of any other credible information in support of Monsieur’s position to
cancel the arrears, the past child support will be confirmed in accordance to
the interim judgments. Monsieur’s demands cannot be granted in that matter.

[
40
]

Finally, Madame asks
this Court to
order that, from January 2018 onward,
Monsieur pay special expenses in the amount of $1,000 per month. Unfortunately,
the Court is not convinced of the actual expenses
as Madame did not present any appropriate evidence for
the special expenses ventilated per school, per program and per child, as they
each attend a different institution and facility. Also, some of these expenses
are either paid by the community, either canceled partially or in full by the
service providers because of Madame’s financial situation. The mere fact that
Madame is asking for that well-rounded figure indicates and confirms the lack
of proof in support of this number and the Court will not proceed to make
calculations that should have been filed and properly presented by the parties.
Therefore, no order will be issued on that matter and given that the children
will end all schooling in City A at the latest in June of this year, this conclusion
will only have a very limited negative impact.

[
41
]

All the other financial
consequences of the divorce are already successfully resolved by the parties.
Their forms establishing the family patrimony and the matrimonial regime show,
with a few exceptions, that there is almost nothing to divide. Monsieur’s
allegation that Madame still has $20,000 in furniture was not supported by
evidence and on the contrary, the Court understands that Monsieur had actually
retrieved all the property to both parties’ satisfaction when he had rented a
truck and taken away his belongings and furniture quite some time ago.

[
42
]

As for the acquests, Madame
failed to induce any evidence that [Company F] value is in vicinity of the $350,000
as she alleges. On the contrary, the proof, on the balance of probabilities
shows that this company is inactive and does not possess any assets. Even if Madame
asks to reserve her rights with regards to that question, the Court finds it
more appropriate to decide this issue at this, last, stage of the litigation.

[
43
]

The only remaining item
is the family van, a Toyota Sienna 2010, which is part of the family patrimony
and property of Monsieur. Madame states its value at $5,000 and Monsieur, $9,000.
The Court will accept Madame’s figure as it is to her disadvantage. Since she
is being granted custody of all four children, she will continue having the
right to use this car until she leaves for Israel. In theory, she is entitled to
half of its value, as her part of the family patrimony, which amounts to $2,500.
In view of this and since she will have the use of this van for four months, it
is only fair that this exclusive use compensates the payment of the half of the
value of the family patrimony. Consequently, Monsieur will not have to pay
anything to Madame with that respect.

[
44
]

Each party blames the
other for the loss of the family residence and the repossession by the bank. Obviously
the animosity between Monsieur and Madame must have blinded them and prevented
the parties from realizing the full financial potential of this house in which
they invested quite a lot in renovations. Nothing can be ordered in that
matter.

[
45
]

As for all the other
requests, with regards to documents, jewellery, personal belongings,
photographs and ceremonial objects, the Court has no evidence what exactly was
in possession of whom, when and who the rightful owner was. Both parties
mutually accuse each other of keeping and even stealing property or not
allowing to retrieve it, while in the other’s possession. Yet, both parties
fail to give any specific and credible evidence on what was kept or is not
returned, and in what circumstances. Both parties deny vigorously any
wrongdoing to that effect. Therefore, the Court cannot issue any type of order
with regards to any object, document or belonging.

[
46
]

In sum, there is
nothing left to be divided.

Emigration to Israel

Principles

[
47
]

The Supreme Court of Canada in the leading
case on the subject of a parent moving abroad,
Gordon
v.
Goertz
, has
determined the applicable test
:

[49] The law can be summarized as
follows:

1. The parent applying for a change in the custody or access order
must meet the threshold requirement of demonstrating a material change in the
circumstances affecting the child.

2. If the threshold is met, the judge on the application must
embark on a fresh inquiry into what is in the best interests of the child,
having regard to all the relevant circumstances relating to the child's needs
and the ability of the respective parents to satisfy them.

3. This inquiry is based on the findings of the judge who made the
previous order and evidence of the new circumstances.

4. The inquiry does not begin with a legal presumption in favour
of the custodial parent, although the custodial parent's views are entitled to
great respect.

5. Each case turns on its own unique circumstances.  The only
issue is the best interest of the child in the particular circumstances of the
case.

6. The focus is on the best interests of the child, not the
interests and rights of the parents.

7. More particularly the judge should consider,
inter alia
:

(a) the existing custody arrangement and relationship between the
child and the custodial parent;

(b) the existing access arrangement and the relationship between
the child and the access parent;

(c) the desirability of maximizing contact between the child and
both parents;

(d) the views of the child;

(e) the custodial parent’s reason for moving,
only
in the
exceptional case where it is relevant to that parent’s ability to meet the
needs of the child;

(f) disruption to the child of a change in custody;

(g) disruption to the child consequent on removal from family, schools,
and the community he or she has come to know.

[
50] In the end,
the importance of the child remaining with the parent to whose custody it has
become accustomed in the new location must be weighed against the continuance
of full contact with the child's access parent, its extended family and its
community.  The ultimate question in every case is this:  what is in
the best interests of the child in all the circumstances, old as well as new?

[16]

[
48
]

In
Droit de la famille — 171821
, the Court of Appeal reiterated the analytical framework applicable
in the event of the relocation of a parent :

[27]

Dans l’arrêt de principe
Gordon
c. Goertz
, la Cour suprême préconise, pour l’étude d’une demande de
modification de l’ordonnance de garde ou d’accès résultant d’un déménagement
d’un des parents, une analyse en deux étapes. La première étape consiste à
vérifier si un changement important est survenu. En l’absence d’un changement
significatif, l’exercice s’arrête là. Si un changement important est survenu,
le juge se prononce sur la nouvelle situation et décide de la garde dans le
meilleur intérêt de l’enfant.(…)

La deuxième étape de l’analyse

[33]

À cette étape,
« […] le juge doit de nouveau déterminer l’intérêt de l’enfant en tenant
compte de toutes les circonstances pertinentes relativement aux besoins de
l’enfant et à la capacité de chacun des parents d’y pourvoir ». Dans
Gordon
,
la Cour suprême énumère un certain nombre non limitatif de facteurs à
considérer :

[49]
[…]
6.  L'accent est mis sur
l'intérêt de l'enfant et non sur l'intérêt et les droits des parents.

7.  Plus
particulièrement, le juge devrait tenir compte notamment des éléments suivants:

a)    l'entente de garde déjà
conclue et la relation actuelle entre l'enfant et le parent gardien;

b)    l'entente déjà conclue
sur le droit d'accès et la relation actuelle entre l'enfant et le parent qui
exerce ce droit;

c)    l'avantage de maximiser
les contacts entre l'enfant et les deux parents;

d)    l'opinion de l'enfant;

e)    la raison pour laquelle
le parent gardien déménage,
uniquement
dans le cas exceptionnel où
celle-ci a un rapport avec la capacité du parent de pourvoir aux besoins de
l'enfant;

f)     la perturbation
que peut causer chez l'enfant une modification de la garde;

g)
la perturbation que peut causer chez l'enfant l'éloignement de sa famille, des
écoles et du milieu auxquels il s'est habitué.

[Soulignement
dans l’original]

[34]

La
formulation de la question est simple : à quel parent confier la garde
dans l’intérêt de l’enfant? Si la question est incontournable, la réponse n’est
pas toujours évidente, lorsque, comme en l’espèce, la capacité parentale des
parties est, selon la juge, équipollente. Les juges sont conscients du
caractère parfois déchirant d’arrêter un choix entre deux parents en procédant
au difficile examen des facteurs qui penchent tantôt en faveur d’un parent,
tantôt en faveur de l’autre.

Considérations générales

[35]

L’objectif
poursuivi tient à rechercher la solution qui soit dans le plus grand intérêt de
l’enfant. Lorsqu’un changement important est survenu dans la situation de
l’enfant, l’exercice ne vise ni à punir l’un des parents ni à compenser
l’autre, mais à arrêter les modalités de garde qui répondent le mieux à la
finalité recherchée.

[17]

(References omitted)

[
49
]

More recently, in
Droit de la famille –
172102
,
while applying this test,
the Court of appeal reversed
the decision of the trial judge who dismissed the request for the mother of the
child to
move

back to France. The mother had met the father in City A during her studies and
from their relationship a child was born. The mother’s return to France with
the child after she had completed her studies was confirmed by the
Court of Appeal :

[48]

Elle [juge de première
instance] devait se demander si sa décision de retourner vivre en France
« repose sur un motif injustifié qui nuit à sa capacité d’agir à titre de
parent» alors qu’elle s’est interrogée quant à la suffisance des efforts
déployés par l’appelante pour se trouver un travail au Québec. Dans
l’éventualité d’une réponse négative à cette question, elle devait tenir pour
acquis le retour de l’appelante en France et se demander à qui confier la garde
exclusive de X, une garde partagée n’étant pas possible dans les circonstances.

[49]

La Cour Suprême a en effet
établi très clairement dans l’affaire
Gordon c. Goertz
que la décision
d’un parent de vivre et de travailler là où il le souhaite doit être respectée
en l’absence de circonstances particulières bien identifiées :

S’il convient de rejeter toute présomption légale en faveur du parent
gardien, il y a toutefois lieu d’accorder le plus grand respect et la plus
grande considération aux opinions du parent gardien, qui vit avec l’enfant et
assume quotidiennement la tâche de prendre des décisions qui sont dans son
intérêt. La décision du parent gardien de vivre et de travailler là où il
l’entend doit elle aussi être respectée, sauf si elle repose sur un motif
injustifié qui nuit à la capacité du parent gardien d’agir à titre de parent.
[18]

(References omitted)

[
50
]

In the same judgment, the Court of Appeal supported
its conclusion by the following comments, that this Court finds of interest
to the case at hand :

[52]

Cette décision de retourner en
France est compréhensible et apparaît rationnelle. Il ne s’agit ni d’un caprice
ni d’une façon de punir l’intimé ou d’autrement le priver de son fils. Il
s’agit d’une situation difficile où l’un et l’autre des parents ont de bonnes
raisons de vouloir vivre dans le pays où ils ont grandi et où ils ont des liens
d’attachement importants.

[53]

L’appelante n’est venue au
Québec que pour y faire des études doctorales. Les circonstances ont fait
qu’elle a rencontré l’intimé, en est tombée amoureuse et a eu un enfant avec
lui. À ce moment, elle désirait bâtir une famille et, dans ce contexte, était
heureuse de demeurer au Québec. La demande de résidence permanente qu’elle a
déposée était d’ailleurs appuyée par le parrainage de l’intimé.

[54]

La situation est toute autre
une fois les parties séparées. Sans même prendre en compte les difficultés que
l’appelante pourrait avoir à obtenir un permis lui permettant de résider au
Québec de façon permanente — puisqu’elle ne détient qu’un visa post études
valide jusqu’en septembre 2019 — il est suffisant de souligner qu’elle est
seule ici. Quoiqu’elle ait quelques amis au Québec, toute sa famille est en
France. Elle y a grandi et y a ses racines. Ses relations avec la famille de
l’intimé ne sont pas bonnes. Elle vient de terminer ses études et doit
entreprendre sa vie professionnelle. Elle a un enfant dont elle s’occupe
quotidiennement depuis la naissance et souhaite organiser sa vie de façon à
pouvoir concilier ses obligations de mère et celles de sa vie professionnelle.

Application

[
51
]

Here, as well, Madame has no attachment
whatsoever to Quebec. She is an Israeli citizen, born in that country and with
all her family living there. She doesn’t speak French and her knowledge of
English, even though she has been a resident of City A for a decade now, is
only basic. She moved to Canada thanks to the sponsorship of Monsieur but is
still not a Canadian citizen and did not even apply to become one either, which
is a factor supporting the conclusion of her lack of interest to fully
integrate in Canada. Finally, the evidence shows that the parties have planned before
the separation to emigrate to Israel.

[
52
]

Once that finding is made, the next step is to
determine to whom the custody of the four children is given
[19]
; the Court shall either change
custody in favor of Monsieur or allow Madame to relocate in Israel with the
children. With that respect, the Court’s paramount goal is the interest of the
children. In
Droit de la famille — 172882
, the Court of Appeal stated the following factors to take into
consideration:

[6]

En principe, comme l’avait
relevé la Cour dans l’arrêt Droit de la famille
─ 071132, la recherche du meilleur intérêt de
l’enfant passe par l’analyse de nombreux éléments de fait : les besoins de
l’enfant, la capacité parentale d’y répondre, la relation affective entre
l’enfant et les parents ainsi qu’entre lui et les membres de la famille, sa
stabilité, son environnement psychosocial, sa santé physique et mentale de même
que celle de celui qui en revendique la garde, la disponibilité réelle des
parents, leurs habitudes de vie si celles-ci ont une incidence directe sur
l’enfant, la non-séparation de la fratrie, le désir de l’enfant et la
disposition à favoriser la relation avec l’autre parent.
[20]

(Reference omitted)

[
53
]

Monsieur objects to
Madame
emigrating to Israel mainly on three
grounds.

[
54
]

First, he (and his sister) states that the

safety
of his children would be
compromised, as Israel is a very dangerous third world country, and that Madame
intends to live in a bad neighborhood in the City of Kiryat Malachi where one
may find a lot of residents of African descent, that Monsieur qualifies as
“being a lower grade of people” and that it is vulnerable to terrorist attacks.
He filed in his proof several print-outs of websites and newspaper articles
about the dangers of living in Israel and especially in the south.

[
55
]

Second, he alleges that he will lose all
contact with the children if they move to Israel.
He adds that his passport was taken away due
to unpaid child support.

[
56
]

Third, he is afraid that his sons may become victims of
pedophiles either because the father-in-law of a friend of Madame is a
convicted pedophile and because his sons would have to attend
Mikveh
(which is a bath used for the purpose
of
ritual
immersion in Judaism
to achieve
purity
) without
him being present, while this religious activity is a preying ground and lurking
with pedophiles.

[
57
]

He does not allege that social or health
services are not adequate to meet his children’s needs, even the two autistic
sons
. Also, he does not ask to reclaim custody
of his children should Madame emigrate to Israel, he only opposes such a plan.
Yet, there is no other alternative; either the children are with their mother
in Israel, either they stay in City A with Monsieur. On that specific issue, the
Court is convinced by Madame’s testimony to the effect that all four children
will be adequately cared for by the social, educational and health services locally
available.

[
58
]

Monsieur does not oppose the relocation plan on
the ground that Madame will be without means to live comfortably in Israel.
While he questions the cost of living and the possibility for Madame to find
suitable employment, the evidence shows that Madame was offered a job in Israel
by an organization where she
used
to work before coming to Canada.
[21]

She will have a decent monthly salary of 8,500 shekels (approximately $3,000)
and will be provided a free cell phone and a car. Moreover, she will not have
to pay tuition, as the religious or rabbinical schools that the children will
attend, are free in Israel. Therefore this motive cannot prevent the Court not
to allow Madame to emigrate with the children.

[
59
]

With regards to the safety concerns, i
n
L.S. v. G.S.
[22]
, the Court of Appeal for British
Columbia confirmed, in a case that also dealt with emigration to Israel, that
it is an important issue to review:

[107]     Mr. S. submits that the trial judge
failed to give any credence to his submission that Israel was a less
safe country in which to raise children than Canada.  He testified that he
had safety concerns when living in Israel before the parties moved to
Canada.

[108]     Mr. S. submits that the trial judge
ignored his concerns and relied, instead, on the evidence of Ms. S.’s father
and brother that they felt safe raising their families in Israel.  In
that respect, Mr. S. refers to para. 60 of the trial judge’s reasons:

Mr. S. is concerned about the family’s security in Israel.
The evidence from Ms. S.’s father and brother who reside there is that they
live a full life without fear.  A. A.i, Ms. S.’s father, says that he is
confident in his safety.  He says that it is very safe in Israel,
particularly in comparison to some other countries.  Mr. A. says he does
not take any additional safety measures.  M. A., Ms. S.’s brother, says
that family life thrives in Israel and is highly valued.

[109]     While there is no reason to doubt
that Ms. S.’s family feels secure in raising a family in Israel, their
feelings are not an answer to Mr. S.’s stated concerns.  It cannot be
gainsaid that Israel is a more dangerous country in which to live
than is Canada. The fact that it may be a safer country to live than “some
other countries” is irrelevant, since the only comparator before the court was
Vancouver.

[110]     Mr. and Ms. S. chose to
leave Israel to live and raise their children in Canada as
Canadians.  The trial judge did not say that Mr. S.’s fears about their
security in Israel were not genuine; rather she seems to have
dismissed them as being of no consequence.  In so doing, I find she erred.
While the relative safety of Canada versus Israel as a place in which
to raise children may not have been a major factor in the trial judge’s
analysis, it was one of many factors relevant to the children’s best interests.

]

matter

[79]

There is also the security
issue.

[80]

While the current situation in
Israel gives cause to worry, the evidence is not such, in the Court’s view, as
to warrant the conclusion that security issues should be reasons to prohibit
the move.

[81]

There has been some turmoil in
Israel in recent months. In fact, throughout its history, the State of Israel
has often been faced with security challenges.

[82]

First of all, in general
terms, it seems outside of the scope of intervention of the Court to hold that,
as a general rule, it would be unsafe for the M. family to move to Israel. The
invitation to caution issued by some governments falls short of evidence that
Israel is not a secure country.

[83]

Secondly, Modi’in is not in
the areas concerned by the warnings.

[84]

Thirdly, the Court is quite
willing to believe Mr. M. when he says that his family will remain cautious and
keep away from risky zones.

[85]

Finally, there is the issue of
X’s learning challenges. Mr. Fr.’s lawyer argues that moving to a foreign
country, out of the stable environment of Town A and of the school, is a strong
argument against allowing X to go to Israel.

[86]

First of all, the parties have
agreed to have the child assessed and Ms F. has undertaken not to move to
Israel before this assessment is completed.

[87]

Secondly, Israel is a
sophisticated country, whose leaders and people value education; it would be
unreasonable to assume that X could not find the same support for his learning
challenges in Israel schools as he does in Town A.

[88]

In summary, the Court is of
the view that the best interests of X warrant that he stay in the custody of
his mother, whether or not she moves to Israel.

[89]

Given all the circumstances,
the Court concludes that the planned move is made for sound reasons, by
responsible people, and is not meant to frustrate Mr. Fr.’s access to X.

[90]

If there is a move, there will
undoubtedly be adjustments for X. However, even with such adjustments, the
Court feels that the physical and emotional needs of X will be better met if he
stays in the custody of his mom.

[23]

[
61
]

Here the evidence presented by Monsieur is anecdotal
and, at best, general. Even if it was to be retained by this Court, it would
only apply to the global situation of the country of Israel and not to the
specifics of the City of Kiryat Malachi and even less to the situation that Madame
and the children would encounter.

[
62
]

As for the second argument, it is true that the
contacts with Monsieur will become rarer but this is the situation of all
parents whose former spouse, who has custody of the children, relocates. This
being said, the relationship that these children will have with their father
depends really on the latter. The access as offered by Madame is generous and
will be ordered. Monsieur can visit Israel anytime he wants and, when there,
have access to the children. The Court is reminded that Monsieur’s parents and
some of his siblings live in Israel and that he used to visit at least once or
twice a year.
[24]
He can also
have extended access rights if he pays the travel costs for the children to fly
to City A. The two two-week periods of access as offered by Madame are in the
best interest of the children, respectful of the school and religious calendar,
and will allow to maximize the contacts with Monsieur. Finally, generous virtual
or electronic access rights will be ordered.
The Court underlines that Israel is a party to the

Hague Convention
[25]

which is a guarantee for Monsieur that he can successfully petition Israeli
courts if a problem arises.

[
63
]

As for the third argument, Monsieur’s contention that his sons
will or may become victims of pedophiles is not supported by the evidence. It
is unimaginable that Madame will let the children in the company of a convicted
pedophile even if this is a stepfather of a friend of hers. The link that Monsieur
and his sister make does not sustain the scrutiny of minimal logic and
preliminary analysis. Also, the sudden concern for the ritual religious baths
while Monsieur calls himself
Chabad “
light”, meaning that he is not extremely observant, is surprising
and should be quieted by Madame’s declaration that her boys will not be
attending these public baths at all.

[
64
]

In sum, the Court finds that once the separation
occurred, Madame’s situation became quite difficult and different from what she
was accustomed. She found herself living in a strange country, not knowing the
language, unable to sustain herself and her children, living off social
assistance and surviving thanks to her community’s generosity. There is no
evidence that Madame’s decision to move back to her homeland is made in bad
faith or to punish Monsieur and, on the contrary, appears quite well-founded.

[
65
]

The paramount interest of the children dictates that they stay in the
custody of their mother, even if she relocates to Israel. Her plan is
reasonable and made for sound reasons. She wants to work as a teacher (which
she couldn’t do in City A), live in her homeland as an Orthodox Jew, raise the
children accordingly and be surrounded by her family. She will be authorized to
relocate after the school year end in order to minimize any perturbation to the
children.
